claims.text: Adding chromium, molybdenum, and nickel to steel promotes formation of a passive surface film enriched in those elements.
A Cr-, Mo-, and Ni-enriched passive film significantly improves the corrosion resistance of steel in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The initial material is standard carbon or low-alloy steel representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Increasing Cr, Mo, and Ni content will enrich the passive film in Cr, Mo, and Ni.
The enriched passive film acts as an electrochemical barrier.
The enriched passive film reduces the local corrosion current.
The enriched passive film stabilizes the steel surface in harsh environments.
The enriched passive film prevents oxidation and pitting.
Steel with increased Cr, Mo, and Ni will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than the baseline steel under the same exposure conditions.
Steel with increased Cr, Mo, and Ni will exhibit delayed initiation of pitting relative to the baseline steel.
XPS will reveal enrichment of Cr, Mo, and Ni in the passive film of the modified steel.
Conventionally alloyed baseline steels do not form a highly enriched passive film.
The absence of a highly enriched passive film causes baseline steels to exhibit higher corrosion rates.
The proposed mechanism should operate in moderately aggressive acidic, chloride-containing, and elevated-temperature environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear applications.
At exceptionally high temperatures, pressures, or corrosive-agent concentrations, additional degradation mechanisms may dominate and limit applicability of the hypothesis.
Microstructural changes and manufacturing impurities may also influence corrosion behavior.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the film prevents pitting, whereas the predicted outcome only claims delayed pitting initiation; prevention and delay are not equivalent unless a test duration or qualified meaning of prevention is specified.
